## Introduction

<!-- Problem background and overview of the approach. -->

Handwriting styles are highly individual-specific and evolve through years of practice, making them a distinctive but subtle biometric trait. Writer identification from handwritten samples has practical applications in forensic document examination, authorship attribution, and biometric authentication [@Abushahla2026]. The development and improvement in machine learning (ML) techniques has made it possible to learn stylistic features from raw images, and prompts the exploration of the handwritten images in this report.

This report uses a dataset of 25,000 images of handwritten digits (0-4), contributed by 20 writers over 5 sessions, with 50 samples per digit and session. The dataset structure introduces both within- and between-session variation, and shapes the choice of training, validation and testing strategy. 
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a class of neural networks designed to hierarchically learn spatial features from image data [@Reza2026; @Yamashita2018]. Convolutional layers apply filters to learn local patterns such as stroke edges and curves; pooling layers summarises these features into lower dimensions, retaining the most important information while reducing the influence of small changes in feature placement. These feature maps or embeddings are then passed to fully connected layers which map them to class probabilities. In this application, the CNN is trained to answer: which writer produced this image?

Siamese neural networks (SNNs) reframe this question. Rather than assigning an image to a writer, a SNN takes two images and asks: were these written by the same person? Each input is sent simultaneuously through identical CNN subnetworks which produce a learned embedding, a vector representation of the writer style, and outputs the distance between the embeddings within this space. The network is trained to encourage same-writer images to have embeddings close together and push different-writer embeddings further apart, using a contrastive or triplet loss function. A threshold on the embedding distance then converts it into a binary classification of same/different [@He2025]. Originally developed for signature verification [@Bromley1993] and fingerprint verification [@Baldi1993], SNNs are well-suited for handwriting matching, since they learn a series of stylistic features that capture writer similarity, rather than learning a fixed set (), which can then be generalised to unseen writers.
Together, the CNN and SNN when applied to this dataset, will provide richer information on how these ML techniques characterise individual writing styles. This report explores the dataset, builds and evaluates both architectures, compares the strengths and limitations of their performance, and evaluates how this performance varies across different hyperparameter setups, different sessions and across different digits.

The analysis was conducted in R version 4.6.1 [@R]. Both CNNs and Siamese networks were fitted using the Keras framework via the *keras3* R package [@keras3] using the TensorFlow backend [@tensorflow]. The tidyverse package [@tidyverse] was utilised throughout the analysis for data manipulation and plotting using *ggplot2.*
